Kidderminster
KID-ur-min-stur
n. (the Worcestershire carpet town where Richard Baxter ministered from 1641 to 1660 and catechised eight hundred families house by house)
Old English Chideminstre, the minster or church of Cydda; the town later famous for its carpet weaving.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Kidderminster is the Worcestershire town on the Stour, and it is the most instructive parish in English pastoral history. Richard Baxter came as lecturer in 1641 to a town he described as ignorant, rude and reviling, with a drunken curate and a people who scarcely knew the catechism; apart from the war years he stayed until 1660. His method was deliberate and he published it. He preached twice on the Lord's day and once in the week; he and his assistant spent two whole days every week in private catechising, taking the families of the parish in turn, an hour to a family, going through the catechism and then applying it personally to each member; in this way the eight hundred families of the parish came round once a year. He found a church where the galleries had to be built to hold the hearers. Out of the experience came The Reformed Pastor in 1656, written for a ministers' meeting and the sharpest book on the ministry in English. Baxter's own doctrine of justification was faulty and the dictionary says so; his pastoral method it commends without reservation.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a pastor as a minister having the care of a church; to catechise as to instruct by question and answer; the counsel of God as his revealed purpose; to shun as to avoid; and sincerity as freedom from hypocrisy.

expand to see more

PASTOR, n. A shepherd; one that has the care of flocks and herds; a minister of the gospel who has the charge of a church.

CATECHISE, v.t. To instruct by asking questions and correcting the answers; to instruct in the principles of religion.

COUNSEL, n. Advice; deliberation; in theology, the revealed purpose and will of God.

SHUN, v.t. To avoid; to keep clear of; to refuse to meet or encounter; to neglect.

SINCERITY, n. Honesty of mind or intention; freedom from simulation or hypocrisy; purity of purpose.

Key Scripture

Act 20:20 — "And how I kept back nothing that was profitable unto you, but have shewed you, and have taught you publickly, and from house to house,"

Act 20:27 — "For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God."

1Ti 4:16 — "Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee."

2Co 4:2 — "But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God."

Modern Corruption

Worcestershire town where Richard Baxter ministered from 1641 to 1660, catechising the parish's eight hundred families house by house two days a week, and out of which The Reformed Pastor came in 1656.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that preaching from a pulpit is only half the pastoral office and that the other half is conducted at kitchen tables. Baxter's discovery at Kidderminster, which he pressed on every minister he could reach, was that he had preached for years to people who could not have stated the first article of the faith, and that an hour's private examination did more for a family than a year of sermons heard at a distance. Paul claims to have done both at Ephesus and names the second explicitly: “have taught you publickly, and from house to house” (Act 20:20). He also claims completeness, that “I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27), which is a standard a man can only know he has met if he has gone through the whole of it with people one by one.

The second thing to recover is that the method binds the minister before it binds the people. Baxter put himself and his assistant under two full days of catechising a week for the sake of eight hundred families, and he wrote The Reformed Pastor to tell other ministers that they were not doing their work. Paul's charge joins the man and the doctrine in one clause and makes the pastor's own soul part of the business: “Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee” (1Ti 4:16). The manner is to be open, with nothing managed and nothing held back, for the apostle renounced “the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully” (2Co 4:2). The dictionary records that Baxter's own account of justification, with its place for faith and evangelical obedience as a personal righteousness, is an error that his admirers must not take with the method; and that the method, taken by itself, has never been bettered in England.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek kat' oikous sense of house to house in Acts 20; Greek boule (G1012), counsel or purpose; Greek epecho (G1907), to take heed.

expand to see more

Greek didasko (G1321) — to teach, to instruct; “and have taught you publickly, and from house to house”, Acts 20:20.

Greek hupostello (G5288) — to draw back, to keep back, to shun; “I kept back nothing that was profitable unto you”, Acts 20:20.

Greek boule (G1012) — counsel, purpose, determination; “to declare unto you all the counsel of God”, Acts 20:27.

Greek epecho (G1907) — to hold upon, to take heed to; “Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine”, 1 Timothy 4:16.

Greek doloo (G1389) — to adulterate, to handle deceitfully; “nor handling the word of God deceitfully”, 2 Corinthians 4:2.

Usage

"“and have taught you publickly, and from house to house” (Act 20:20) — two full days of catechising a week."

"“all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27) — eight hundred families round once a year."

"“Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine” (1Ti 4:16) — The Reformed Pastor, 1656."
